name: Theyyam season (North Malabar)
tagline: Thulam season of living god-performances across North Malabar
summary: Theyyam season opens in Thulam (late Oct–Nov) across Kannur and Kasaragod and runs through the spring months; village kavus present vivid ritual dances, colour and community rites.
description: Theyyam (also called kaliyattam) is a living ritual performance tradition of North Malabar: painted performers, tall headgear (kolam), drumming and trance-persona embody local deities and ancestral spirits.
It matters because Theyyam is both ritual and community theatre — the kavus (sacred groves and temple-shrines) keep local history, caste stories and seasonal calendars alive and public.

For visitors the season offers vivid early-morning and evening performances, close contact with ritual practitioners, and a rich calendar that moves from village to village across Kannur and Kasaragod.
Dates and performances are set by each kavu’s committee; always confirm a shrine’s day before you travel because the rota and local decisions determine what appears on any given night.
highlights: Season opens in Thulam (Malayalam month, late Oct–Nov) and runs into the spring months; peak activity Jan–Apr.
Intense kolam (face & body paint), towering crowns and fire rituals — visually striking and unlike stage dance.
Hundreds of distinct Theyyam forms and dozens of active kavus across Kannur and Kasaragod.
Close, communal setting — spectators stand at the edge of the ritual ground; offerings and blessings are part of the experience.
Local calendars (DTPC, community sites) list day-by-day venues — confirm by phone or at the kavu.

sections.heading: Background
body: Theyyam is a ritual theatre system practised mainly in northern Kerala (Kannur and Kasaragod). Each performance honours a local deity, ancestor or guardian spirit and blends costume, music, dramatic action and oracular speech.
Seasonality is central: communities mount kaliyattam (kavu festivals) on fixed days of the Malayalam calendar. The public role of Theyyam links agriculture, local justice, memory and community bonds.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a full Theyyam kaliyattam (often an all‑day affair) to see preliminary drumming and vellaattam (preparatory form), the kolam reveal, trance sequences and blessings. Popular forms include Vettakkorumakan, Chamundi, Kalichan and regional variants — each kavu announces which kolams will appear.

Respect local rules: follow the kavu committee’s directions about where to stand, do not cross ritual lines, ask before photographing close-up, and be mindful that these are living worship acts rather than tourist spectacles.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Plan around local calendars: official and community calendars (DTPC Kannur, independent Theyyam calendars and local Facebook/Malayalam groups) publish daily schedules during the season, but shrine committees make the final call — always confirm by phone or on arrival.

Logistics: base yourself in Kannur, Payyannur, Kanhangad or Kasaragod and travel to nearby kavus; performances commonly take place early morning and evening. Confirm timings and accessibility in advance; the ground is often earthen and barefoot is usual for participants.

latest.text: Community calendars and local reports show the 2026–27 Theyyam season beginning in Thulam with confirmed performances across Kasaragod and Kannur in early November.
Coverage and tourism guides for the 2026 season note that district and community calendars are now active and that DTPC Kannur is coordinating a partial seasonal listing for visitors.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Thulam (Malayalam month; late Oct–Nov) through the spring months — peak January–April; confirm specific shrine dates.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Base in Kannur, Payyannur, Kanhangad or Kasaragod (rail + road). From these towns take local transport to village kavus; timings and access vary by site — confirm before you travel.
etiquette: Confirm the kavu’s date and arrival time by phone or local tourism office before you set out.
Follow kavu rules: watch where officials ask you to stand, ask before photographing, and respect ritual boundaries and offerings.
Wear modest clothing and be prepared for uneven, dusty or muddy ground; carry ear protection if near the drums.
Hire a local guide or consult the district tourism office / trusted Theyyam calendars for translations and context.
